title: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
summary: Behaviour prevention on endpoint evaluates what a process actually does rather than what it looks like, and blocks activity that matches attack patterns in progress. The mechanism collects operating system telemetry such as process creation with command lines, file and registry writes, network connections and script content, applies heuristic rules, models or analytics to decide whether a sequence is suspicious, then intervenes by terminating the process, blocking the action or quarantining an artefact. Real environments run it as the prevention layer of an endpoint agent, often alongside ransomware canary files, credential theft protection and script control, all managed from a central console. Evidence is the alert or block record itself, which normally includes the process tree, the user, the file hash and the reason the rule fired, and these records support both response and tuning. The misunderstandings are that behavioural detection replaces signature scanning, when the two catch different things, and that a blocked alert closes the incident, when a high severity block usually marks one visible step of a longer intrusion that still needs scoping across the estate.

beginner.definition: Behaviour prevention on endpoint watches what programs actually do on a computer. Instead of only checking known bad files, it looks at actions such as deleting many documents or reading saved passwords. When a program behaves like an attack, the system stops it.
beginner.whyItMatters: New malware often looks different from anything seen before. File signatures may not recognise it at all. Behaviour rules catch the actions an attacker must take anyway, such as encrypting files or stealing credentials. That gives you a chance to stop an intrusion which would otherwise pass every list based check.
howItWorks: An agent on the computer records actions such as program starts, file changes and network use.
Rules and models compare those actions with patterns that usually mean an attack.
When a pattern matches, the agent blocks the action or stops the whole program.
It sends a record to a central console with the process, the user and the reason.
Analysts investigate, tune noisy rules, and hunt for related activity on other machines.
beginner.example: Think of a security guard who watches behaviour rather than faces. A person walking through a shop is normal. The same person filling a bag with goods and heading for the fire exit is not, even if the guard has never seen them before. Behaviour prevention on endpoint is that guard for a computer: it ignores the question of whether the program is known, and asks whether what it is doing makes sense.
takeaways: Behaviour rules catch attacks that signatures miss, so run both rather than choosing one.
A block is a starting point for investigation, not proof that the incident is over.
Tune the rules with process and reason data, or alert fatigue will hide real attacks.

objectives: Explain how behavioural prevention differs from signature based detection.
Describe the endpoint telemetry that behaviour rules rely on.
Interpret a prevention alert using its process tree, user and reason fields.
Recognise which attack stages behavioural controls commonly disrupt.
Plan tuning and response steps after a high severity block.
